metadata.title: Can You Trust a Generator Tested on Its Own Data?
metadata.note: SurveyMind project-progress video. This week's real content: with SurveyMind's described generation method still blocked, work shifted to designing an independent synthetic-data generator. Before any code was written, identified and resolved a circularity risk — a generator fit and validated on the same data would trivially pass the congruence test regardless of quality. Decision: 80/20 train/test split, generator fit only on training data, validated only against held-out test data. Pressure-tested and strengthened: (1) derived that the 120,664-respondent held-out test portion gives correlation-estimate standard error ~0.003, versus Week 2's synthetic-side n=200 (~0.07, 20x less precise) — confirming no asymptotic-fragility risk here; (2) set an explicit leakage boundary for the next decision (choosing the generative method) — that choice may draw on external literature or the training portion only, never the test portion. Submitted to Gru this week. No generation code written yet — that is next week's work. Built using the same proven pattern set as prior videos: folderLabel set explicitly on ClaudeComposerAsk beats (@HumanitariansAI), OutroCTA used instead of ClaudeTitleOutro, BLUF lines kept short to avoid edge-bleed, no stale sparse_by_design flags except the legitimate BrutalistHesitantWriter typing-beat exemption.

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — HAI persona, world-language hello (short form only)
beats.narration_text: Hi. Can you trust a synthetic data test that was graded on its own homework?

props.command: claude "design a train/test split so a synthetic data generator is validated on data it never saw during fitting"

beats.role_note: MANDATORY — BrutalistHesitantWriter, executive summary, hesitation = the pedagogy
beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. Build a synthetic data generator, then test it against the very same real data it was built from. That sounds like a reasonable check. It isn't — that's circular, not real proof the generator works.

props.text:
Build it, then test it on the same data.
That sounds like a reasonable check.
It isn't. That's circular, not real proof.

qc.sparse_reason: hesitant-writer typing bookend accumulates one line token by token — mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design (documented exemption case in final_frame_check.py)

beats.role_note: vox-style illustration (C2/C3), NOT a build-loop beat
beats.narration_text: Here's the actual risk. If a generator is fit to match a dataset's correlation structure, and then tested against that same dataset, it will always look realistic — even if all it did was memorize the structure it was handed, instead of actually learning anything general.
beats.visual_intent: two cards showing the circularity problem

items.label: Fit on all the data
items.sub: then test on that same data

items.label: Always looks realistic
items.sub: even if it just memorized the structure

beats.act: THE FIX — a genuine test of generalization
beats.visual_intent: simple description card explaining the train/test split fix
beats.narration_text: The fix: split the real data before building anything. Fit the generator only on the training portion. Test it only against data it never saw. That's what makes the result a genuine test of generalization, not a circular one.

lines: Split the real data before building anything.
Fit the generator on the training portion only.
Test it only against data it never saw.
That's a genuine test of generalization.

beats.act: THE PIPELINE — how the split actually works
beats.narration_text: As a pipeline: the real 603,322 respondents get split, 80% for training, 20% held out. The generator is fit only on the training portion. The held-out portion is never touched until validation — then the existing pipeline checks the generator's output against it.
beats.visual_intent: four-stage flow diagram from the real dataset to a held-out validation step

props.title: Split First, Trust What's Unseen
props.footerNote: the generator never sees the test portion, ever
props.sparkLine: Split first. Trust what's left unseen.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: UI appears because the interface IS the subject here
beats.narration_text: Before trusting this design, it got checked. The held-out portion holds about a hundred twenty thousand respondents — correlation estimates there are stable to about three thousandths. Compare that to a real fragility risk from a few weeks back: a synthetic sample of just two hundred, twenty times less precise. This split isn't fragile.
beats.visual_intent: verdict artifact page comparing the two sample sizes and their precision

beats.role_note: the lesson, honest about scope — sets up next week's decision
beats.narration_text: One thing still had to be nailed down before moving on. Choosing the actual generative method comes next — and that choice can't be informed by peeking at the held-out test data. Only the training portion, or outside literature, are fair game. That boundary is set now, before the method gets picked, not after.

lines: Choosing the method comes next, not now.
It can't be informed by the test portion.
Only training data or outside literature.
That boundary is set before the method is chosen.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — ClaudeComposerAsk, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.', prompt read and discussed aloud
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're validating anything you built from data, check whether your test set ever touched the fitting step. If it did, your result might be circular, not real. Ask Claude to help you check before you trust the number.
